Jesus enters Jerusalem (verses 1–11)

Jesus' remarkable entrance into the city showed that he did not fear the strength or malice of his enemies.

The disciples were frightened, so this would encourage them.

Christ was not overwhelmed by the suffering he knew awaited him.

Yet everything about the entry displayed his humility.

We should avoid seeking personal grandeur and willingly associate with people of modest circumstances.

How inappropriate for Christians to demand splendor when Christ deliberately rejected it!

The crowd welcomed him as the One who was to come, long promised and expected.

He came in the Lord's name.

Let us give him our best affections.

He is the blessed Savior who brings blessing, and the Father who sent him deserves our praise.

Glory to God in the highest heavens, blessed forever!

The fruitless fig tree and the temple (verses 12–18)

Jesus examined the fig tree seeking fruit.

The ordinary time for figs had not yet fully come, though it was approaching.

He found none.

The tree was made a warning not to other trees but to the people of that generation.

Henry sees it as a figure of judgment on the Jewish religious community of Jesus' day, in which Christ sought fruit but found none.

That is his historical interpretation rather than an assertion about every Jewish person.

Jesus then entered the temple and corrected the abuses taking place in its courts.

It showed that when the Redeemer came to Zion he would turn ungodliness away from Jacob.

The chief priests and scribes responded by looking for a way to kill Jesus rather than seeking reconciliation with him.

They must have feared that they were, in effect, fighting against God.

Prayer, faith and forgiveness (verses 19–26)

The disciples were astonished that the fig tree had withered so quickly.

Henry applies it again to people who reject Christ and to his historical reading of the Jewish church's condition.

We should never be satisfied with religion that does not produce good works.

Jesus taught his disciples to pray with faith.

Genuine Christian faith works great spiritual miracles.

It justifies us and thereby removes mountains of guilt, never to rise again in judgment against us.

It purifies the heart and removes mountains of sinful corruption, clearing the way for God's grace to transform our lives.

One principal reason to approach the throne of grace is to seek forgiveness of our sins.

That concern should occupy us every day.

Jesus challenges the religious authorities (verses 27–33)

Jesus showed the close relationship between his own teaching and baptism and John the Baptist's mission.

Both pointed toward establishing the gospel kingdom.

The elders who questioned Jesus were not sincerely seeking truth.

They wanted to win an argument.

He therefore did not owe them the explanation they pretended to desire.

Even without his direct reply, his works clearly demonstrated divine authority.

No human being could have performed those miracles unless God was with him.

The barren fig-tree cursed, The temple cleansed.
(12-18)
Prayer in faith. | (19-26) |
The priests and elders questioned concerning John the Baptist. | (27-33) |
Verses 1-11
Christ's coming into Jerusalem thus remarkably, shows that he was not afraid of the power and malice of his enemies. This would encourage his disciples who were full of fear. Also, that he was not disquieted at the thoughts of his approaching sufferings. But all marked his humiliation; and these matters teach us not to mind high things, but to condescend to those of low estate. How ill it becomes Christians to take state, when Christ was so far from claiming it! They welcomed his person; Blessed is he that cometh, the "He that should come," so often promised, so long expected; he comes in the name of the Lord. Let him have our best affections; he is a blessed Saviour, and brings blessings to us, and blessed be He that sent him. Praises be to our God, who is in the highest heavens, over all, God blessed for ever.
[Mark.11.12-Mark.11.18]
Verses 12-18
Christ looked to find some fruit, for the time of gathering figs, though it was near, was not yet come; but he found none. He made this fig-tree an example, not to the trees, but to the men of that generation. It was a figure of the doom upon the Jewish church, to which he came seeking fruit, but found none. Christ went to the temple, and began to reform the abuses in its courts, to show that when the Redeemer came to Zion, it was to turn away ungodliness from Jacob. The scribes and the chief priests sought, not how they might make their peace with him, but how they might destroy him. A desperate attempt, which they could not but fear was fighting against God.
[Mark.11.19-Mark.11.26]
Verses 19-26
The disciples could not think why that fig-tree should so soon wither away; but all wither who reject Christ; it represented the state of the Jewish church. We should rest in no religion that does not make us fruitful in good works. Christ taught them from hence to pray in faith. It may be applied to that mighty faith with which all true Christians are endued, and which does wonders in spiritual things. It justifies us, and so removes mountains of guilt, never to rise up in judgment against us. It purifies the heart, and so removes mountains of corruption, and makes them plain before the grace of God. One great errand to the throne of grace is to pray for the pardon of our sins; and care about this ought to be our daily concern.
[Mark.11.27-Mark.11.33]
Verses 27-33
Our Saviour shows how near akin his doctrine and baptism were to those of John; they had the same design and tendency, to bring in the gospel kingdom. These elders did not deserve to be taught; for it was plain that they contended not for truth, but victory: nor did he need to tell them; for the works he did, told them plainly he had authority from God; since no man could do the miracles which he did, unless God were with him.

The vineyard and its wicked tenants (verses 1–12)

Through the parable, Jesus taught that God would set aside the Jewish church of his day as an outward institution that had rejected him.

The treatment faithful ministers have received in many ages is shameful.

Some have been persecuted by people who enjoyed religious privileges but failed to produce the corresponding fruit.

At last God sent his beloved Son.

We might expect people to honor someone whom the master himself loved.

Instead the tenants hated the Son precisely because he was the heir.

Christ's exaltation was the Lord's doing.

It is also God who raises up Christ in our hearts and establishes his rule there.

When he does so, it is wonderful to us.

Scripture, faithful preachers and above all Christ's incarnation summon us to honor God through our lives.

Sinners should beware of a proud, worldly attitude.

Those who mock or despise Christ's faithful ministers show the kind of reception they would have given Christ himself if they had met him during his earthly ministry.

The question about taxes (verses 13–17)

Christ's opponents pretended to seek guidance about duty, but their real purpose was to obtain an answer they could use to accuse him.

One of the most dangerous traps for Jesus' followers is becoming absorbed in worldly political quarrels.

Jesus escaped by directing them to recognize the civil obligations their nation had already accepted.

Everyone marveled at the wisdom of his answer.

Many praise the beauty or cleverness of a sermon without obeying its teaching.

Jesus teaches the resurrection (verses 18–27)

A correct understanding of Scripture—the fountain and foundation of revealed religion—is our best protection against error.

The Sadducees mocked the doctrine of resurrection.

Jesus corrected them by explaining the difference between earthly marriage and life in heaven.

Although marriage was established in the first earthly paradise, it will not continue in the heavenly one in the same way.

We create absurd ideas when we try to explain the world of spirits entirely through the arrangements of our present bodily life.

It would make no sense for the living God to remain the eternal portion and happiness of someone who had ceased to exist forever.

Thus Abraham's soul continues to exist and act, though for a time it is separated from his body.

Those who deny resurrection are seriously mistaken.

Let us pass through this dying world with a joyful expectation of eternal happiness and a glorious resurrection.

The greatest commandment (verses 28–34)

Jesus willingly teaches those who genuinely wish to understand God's will.

He explained that the greatest commandment, which contains all others in principle, is to love God with the whole heart.

When such love governs the soul, it creates a willingness to fulfill every other duty and to do what pleases him.

The old sacrificial offerings only pictured atonement for disobedience to God's moral law.

They were not themselves effective apart from repentance and faith in the promised Savior, producing moral obedience.

Since we have failed to love God and our neighbors in this way and have often done the opposite, we are condemned sinners in need of repentance and mercy.

Christ approved the scribe's understanding and encouraged him.

The man was well placed to go further.

Knowledge of God's law awakens conviction, leads toward repentance and the awareness of needing mercy, and enables us to understand justification through Christ.

David's Son and David's Lord (verses 35–40)

When we understand Scripture's teaching about Christ's person and offices, we are led to confess him as our Lord and God and obey him as the exalted Redeemer.

If ordinary people receive these truths gladly while the educated and powerful oppose them, the first have reason for joy and the second for pity.

Sin concealed beneath a display of piety is doubled wickedness and will meet an especially serious judgment.

Jesus praises the poor widow (verses 41–44)

Jesus still watches what his people give.

He knows both the amount and the motives.

He sees whether our gifts come from love for him or from a wish to be admired.

Many people would criticize the poor widow's offering.

Few would willingly imitate her.

Yet Christ commended her, so we know her action was good and wise.

At the final judgment, modest efforts of poor people to honor their Savior will receive his approval, while magnificent works of unbelievers done from wrong motives will be exposed as worthless.

Verses 1-12
Christ showed in parables, that he would lay aside the Jewish church. It is sad to think what base usage God's faithful ministers have met with in all ages, from those who have enjoyed the privileges of the church, but have not brought forth fruit answerable. God at length sent his Son, his Well-beloved; and it might be expected that he whom their Master loved, they also should respect and love; but instead of honouring him because he was the Son and Heir, they therefore hated him. But the exaltation of Christ was the Lord's doing; and it is his doing to exalt him in our hearts, and to set up his throne there; and if this be done, it cannot but be marvellous in our eyes. The Scriptures, and faithful preachers, and the coming of Christ in the flesh, call on us to render due praise to God in our lives. Let sinners beware of a proud, carnal spirit; if they revile or despise the preachers of Christ, they would have done so their Master, had they lived when he was upon earth.
[Mark.12.13-Mark.12.17]
Verses 13-17
The enemies of Christ would be thought desirous to know their duty, when really they hoped that which soever side he took of the question, they might find occasion to accuse him. Nothing is more likely to insnare the followers of Christ, than bringing them to meddle with disputes about worldly politics. Jesus avoided the snare, by referring to the submission they had already made as a nation; and all that heard him, marvelled at the great wisdom of his answer. Many will praise the words of a sermon, who will not be commanded by the doctrines of it.
[Mark.12.18-Mark.12.27]
Verses 18-27
A right knowledge of the Scripture, as the fountain whence all revealed religion now flows, and the foundation on which it is built, is the best preservative against error. Christ put aside the objection of the Sadducees, who were the scoffing infidels of that day, by setting the doctrine of the future state in a true light. The relation between husband and wife, though appointed in the earthly paradise, will not be known in the heavenly one. It is no wonder if we confuse ourselves with foolish errors, when we form our ideas of the world of spirits by the affairs of this world of sense. It is absurd to think that the living God should be the portion and happiness of a man if he is for ever dead; and therefore it is certain that Abraham's soul exists and acts, though now for a time separate from the body. Those that deny the resurrection greatly err, and ought to be told so. Let us seek to pass through this dying world, with a joyful hope of eternal happiness, and of a glorious resurrection.
[Mark.12.28-Mark.12.34]
Verses 28-34
Those who sincerely desire to be taught their duty, Christ will guide in judgment, and teach his way. He tells the scribe that the great commandment, which indeed includes all, is, that of loving God with all our hearts. Wherever this is the ruling principle in the soul, there is a disposition to every other duty. Loving God with all our heart, will engage us to every thing by which he will be pleased. The sacrifices only represented the atonements for men's transgressions of the moral law; they were of no power except as they expressed repentance and faith in the promised Saviour, and as they led to moral obedience. And because we have not thus loved God and man, but the very reverse, therefore we are condemned sinners; we need repentance, and we need mercy. Christ approved what the scribe said, and encouraged him. He stood fair for further advance; for this knowledge of the law leads to conviction of sin, to repentance, to discovery of our need of mercy, and understanding the way of justification by Christ.
[Mark.12.35-Mark.12.40]
Verses 35-40
When we attend to what the Scriptures declare, as to the person and offices of Christ, we shall be led to confess him as our Lord and God; to obey him as our exalted Redeemer. If the common people hear these things gladly, while the learned and distinguished oppose, the former are happy, and the latter to be pitied. And as sin, disguised with a show of piety, is double iniquity, so its doom will be doubly heavy.
[Mark.12.41-Mark.12.44]
Verses 41-44
Let us not forget that Jesus still sees the treasury. He knows how much, and from what motives, men give to his cause. He looks at the heart, and what our views are, in giving alms; and whether we do it as unto the Lord, or only to be seen of men. It is so rare to find any who would not blame this widow, that we cannot expect to find many who will do like to her; and yet our Saviour commends her, therefore we are sure that she did well and wisely. The feeble efforts of the poor to honour their Saviour, will be commended in that day, when the splendid actions of unbelievers will be exposed to contempt.

Jesus foretells the temple's destruction (verses 1–4)

Christ places little value on impressive outward splendor where purity of heart is absent.

He looked with compassion upon ruined souls and wept over them.

We do not read that he mourned in the same way for the destruction of even a magnificent building.

Let this teach us the importance of having a lasting home in heaven, prepared for us through the Holy Spirit's work.

We should seek that preparation earnestly through every appointed means of grace.

Jesus warns against deception and persecution (verses 5–13)

Jesus answered the disciples not chiefly to satisfy curiosity but to direct their consciences and conduct.

When many people are deceived, believers should become more attentive to guarding themselves.

Christ's disciples may enjoy holy peace of mind even when everything around them is confused, provided they do not turn from their duty.

Suffering for Christ should never be allowed to draw them away from him.

Being hated by everyone is a serious trial.

Yet the work God assigned them would continue and prosper.

The servants may be crushed, but the gospel cannot be crushed.

The promised salvation is more than temporary rescue from danger.

It includes everlasting blessedness.

The approaching destruction of Jerusalem (verses 14–23)

Henry understands these warnings as pointing toward Jerusalem's destruction.

He says that rebellion against Rome and persecution of Christians accelerated the disaster, which came less than forty years after Jesus spoke.

The resulting devastation was extraordinary.

Promises that believers will receive strength to persevere fit perfectly alongside warnings not to fall away.

The more seriously we think about these events, the more reason we have to seek refuge in Christ without delay.

For the salvation of our souls, we should be prepared to relinquish every earthly attachment.

The future appearance of Christ (verses 24–27)

The disciples had confused the destruction of Jerusalem with the end of the world.

Jesus corrected that misunderstanding.

Henry distinguishes Jerusalem's tribulation from Christ's later coming and the last judgment.

Jesus foretold the final dissolution of the present arrangement of the world.

He also described his visible appearance in the clouds and the gathering of all the elect to him.

Remain watchful (verses 28–37)

This is the practical application of Jesus' prophetic teaching.

With regard to Jerusalem's destruction, Henry says the disciples should expect it soon.

With regard to the end of the world, they should not try to calculate the time.

No human being knows its day or hour.

Henry says that Christ, in his divinity, could not be ignorant of anything, while divine wisdom was communicated to his human soul according to God's pleasure.

That is his theological explanation of this passage, not a wording added to the biblical text.

The duty in either case is the same: watch and pray.

When Jesus ascended to heaven, he left meaningful work for every servant.

We should continually expect his return and remain at our assigned tasks.

The warning applies both to our individual death and to the general judgment.

We do not know whether our Master will summon us during youth, middle age or old age.

As soon as we are born, we begin moving toward death.

Our chief concern should be that Christ never finds us careless, idle, absorbed in pleasure or neglectful of duty.

His command to all is “Watch!”, so that we may be found in peace, without spot and blameless.

Verses 1-4
See how little Christ values outward pomp, where there is not real purity of heart. He looks with pity upon the ruin of precious souls, and weeps over them, but we do not find him look with pity upon the ruin of a fine house. Let us then be reminded how needful it is for us to have a more lasting abode in heaven, and to be prepared for it by the influences of the Holy Spirit, sought in the earnest use of all the means of grace.
[Mark.13.5-Mark.13.13]
Verses 5-13
Our Lord Jesus, in reply to the disciples' question, does not so much satisfy their curiosity as direct their consciences. When many are deceived, we should thereby be awakened to look to ourselves. And the disciples of Christ, if it be not their own fault, may enjoy holy security and peace of mind, when all around is in disorder. But they must take heed that they are not drawn away from Christ and their duty to him, by the sufferings they will meet with for his sake. They shall be hated of all men: trouble enough! Yet the work they were called to should be carried on and prosper. Though they may be crushed and borne down, the gospel cannot be. The salvation promised is more than deliverance from evil, it is everlasting blessedness.
[Mark.13.14-Mark.13.23]
Verses 14-23
The Jews in rebelling against the Romans, and in persecuting the Christians, hastened their own ruin apace. Here we have a prediction of that ruin which came upon them within less than forty years after this. Such destruction and desolation, that the like cannot be found in any history. Promises of power to persevere, and cautions against falling away, well agree with each other. But the more we consider these things, the more we shall see abundant cause to flee without delay for refuge to Christ, and to renounce every earthly object, for the salvation of our souls.
[Mark.13.24-Mark.13.27]
Verses 24-27
The disciples had confounded the destruction of Jerusalem and the end of the world. This mistake Christ set right, and showed that the day of Christ's coming, and the day of judgment, shall be after that tribulation. Here he foretells the final dissolution of the present frame and fabric of the world. Also, the visible appearance of the Lord Jesus coming in the clouds, and the gathering together of all the elect to him.
[Mark.13.28-Mark.13.37]
Verses 28-37
We have the application of this prophetic sermon. As to the destruction of Jerusalem, expect it to come very shortly. As to the end of the world, do not inquire when it will come, for of that day and that hour knoweth no man. Christ, as God, could not be ignorant of anything; but the Divine wisdom which dwelt in our Saviour, communicated itself to his human soul according to the Divine pleasure. As to both, our duty is to watch and pray. Our Lord Jesus, when he ascended on high, left something for all his servants to do. We ought to be always upon our watch, in expectation of his return. This applies to Christ's coming to us at our death, as well as to the general judgment. We know not whether our Master will come in the days of youth, or middle age, or old age; but, as soon as we are born, we begin to die, and therefore we must expect death. Our great care must be, that, whenever our Lord comes, he may not find us secure, indulging in ease and sloth, mindless of our work and duty. He says to all, Watch, that you may be found in peace, without spot, and blameless.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesChrist anointed at Bethany.1–11The passover, Jesus declares that Judas would betray him.12–21The Lord's supper instituted.22–31Christ's agony in the garden.32–42He is betrayed and taken.43–52Christ before the high priest.53–65Peter denies Christ.66–72
Christ is anointed at Bethany (verses 1–11)

Christ poured out his soul to death for us. Can we regard anything as too precious to give him?

Do we offer him the precious ointment of our finest affections? We should love him with all our hearts, even when others misunderstand or criticize genuine devotion.

Charity toward poor people, though required, does not excuse neglecting particular acts of devotion to Jesus. Christ praised the woman's action and made it known to believers in every generation. Those who honor Christ will be honored by him.

Covetousness ruled Judas. The love of money that he had cherished became the occasion for his betrayal of his Master. The devil adapted his temptation to Judas's ruling desire and overcame him through it.

Sinful people often construct elaborate schemes to achieve their purposes. Yet the very circumstances they regard as helping them succeed will become curses to them in the end.

The Passover and the announcement of betrayal (verses 12–21)

The events surrounding this Passover were not the result of merely human foresight. The Lord knew them before they happened, as he knows everything concerning us.

If we receive him, he will dwell in our hearts.

The Son of Man went toward suffering and death as Scripture had foretold, like a lamb led to slaughter. Nevertheless, the betrayer remained guilty and faced a dreadful judgment.

God's permission of human sin does not compel anyone to sin. Nor does God's ability to bring glory out of wicked actions excuse those who freely commit them or reduce their punishment.

Jesus institutes the Lord's Supper (verses 22–31)

The Lord's Supper is nourishment for the soul. Therefore, only a small quantity of bread and wine is needed for the bodily sign.

Our Master instituted it by his own example and practice. It is to continue until his second coming.

He established it with blessing and thanksgiving, as a remembrance of his death.

The blood of Christ is repeatedly described as the price of our redemption. What comfort for repentant sinners that this blood is shed for many! If it is for many, why should I not seek its benefits myself?

The Supper signifies the communication of the blessings purchased by Christ's death. We should apply the truth of Christ crucified to ourselves, so that it becomes food and drink for the soul, strengthening and refreshing spiritual life.

It also gives an earnest and a foretaste of the happiness of heaven. Enjoying spiritual blessings should weaken our attachment to pleasures of the senses.

Whoever has tasted spiritual delights is led to desire eternal ones.

Although the great Shepherd endured every suffering without a single false step, his followers were scattered by a much smaller measure of suffering.

We are quick to think highly of our own courage and trust our own hearts. Peter should not have answered his Master with such self-confidence, but with fear and trembling.

Lord, give me grace so that I do not deny you.

Christ's agony in Gethsemane (verses 32–42)

Christ's suffering began with what was most painful: the suffering of his soul.

He became deeply amazed and distressed. Mark's words here express his anguish even more forcefully than Matthew's account.

The terrors of God stood before him, and he allowed himself to contemplate them. No sorrow had ever been like his.

He was now made a curse for us. The curses of the law were laid upon him as our Surety. He tasted death in all its bitterness.

His fear was the natural human fear of pain and death, from which human nature recoils.

Can we think lightly of sin when we see what our sins—even though they were only reckoned to him—brought upon Jesus? How can sin weigh so little upon us when it weighed so heavily upon him?

As we look upon the One we pierced, we should mourn over our sin rather than treat it as a small matter.

As man, Christ prayed that, if possible, the suffering might pass from him. As Mediator, he submitted himself completely to the Father's will: not what I will, but what you will.

The disciples' weakness returned and overcame them. Our bodies can weigh heavily upon our souls.

Yet when trouble approaches, we should prepare for it. Even believers can look upon the Redeemer's suffering drowsily: instead of being ready to die with him, they are sometimes unwilling to watch with him for one hour.

Jesus is betrayed and arrested (verses 43–52)

The religious rulers sought to destroy Jesus because he did not appear as an earthly prince. Instead, he preached repentance, reform and holy living and directed people's thoughts, desires and hopes toward the world to come.

Peter wounded one of those who came to arrest Jesus.

It is easier to fight for Christ than to die for him.

Yet there is an important distinction between disciples who fail through weakness and hypocrites. Hypocrites may rashly call Jesus their Master and profess great affection, while delivering him into the hands of his enemies.

By their betrayal, they hurry toward their own destruction.

Jesus stands before the high priest (verses 53–65)

Jesus was condemned before the great Jewish council.

Peter followed, but the fire beside the high priest and the company of the high priest's servants were dangerous places for him. He had entered a temptation.

The council sought false witnesses diligently. Yet even by stretching their law as far as possible, their testimony was insufficient to establish a capital charge.

Jesus was asked whether he was the Son of the Blessed, meaning the Son of God.

He pointed to his second coming as proof of his identity.

The insults and violence directed against him reveal both humanity's hostility toward God and God's freely given, unspeakable love toward humanity.

Peter denies Jesus (verses 66–72)

Peter's denial began when he kept his distance from Christ.

Those ashamed of godliness are already on the path toward denying him.

People who fear spending time among Christ's followers because they might be drawn into suffering with them take a worse risk by spending time with his enemies: there they may be drawn into sin against him.

When crowds admired Jesus, Peter readily acknowledged him. Now, when Jesus was deserted and despised, Peter refused any association with him.

Yet Peter repented very quickly.

Let anyone who thinks he stands be careful not to fall.

And let anyone who has fallen remember Peter, consider their own sins, and return to the Lord with tears and earnest prayer, seeking forgiveness and renewal through the Holy Spirit.

Christ anointed at Bethany. | (1-11) |
The passover, Jesus declares that Judas would betray him. | (12-21) |
The Lord's supper instituted. | (22-31) |
Christ's agony in the garden. | (32-42) |
He is betrayed and taken. | (43-52) |

Verses 1-11
Did Christ pour out his soul unto death for us, and shall we think any thing too precious for him? Do we give him the precious ointment of our best affections? Let us love him with all the heart, though it is common for zeal and affection to be misunderstood and blamed; and remember that charity to the poor will not excuse any from particular acts of piety to the Lord Jesus. Christ commended this woman's pious attention to the notice of believers in all ages. Those who honour Christ he will honour. Covetousness was Judas' master lust, and that betrayed him to the sin of betraying his Master; the devil suited his temptation to that, and so conquered him. And see what wicked contrivances many have in their sinful pursuits; but what appears to forward their plans, will prove curses in the end.
[Mark.14.12-Mark.14.21]
Verses 12-21
Nothing could be less the result of human foresight than the events here related. But our Lord knows all things about us before they come to pass. If we admit him, he will dwell in our hearts. The Son of man goes, as it is written of him, as a lamb to the slaughter; but woe to that man by whom he is betrayed! God's permitting the sins of men, and bringing glory to himself out of them, does not oblige them to sin; nor will this be any excuse for their guilt, or lessen their punishment.
[Mark.14.22-Mark.14.31]
Verses 22-31
The Lord's supper is food for the soul, therefore a very little of that which is for the body, as much as will serve for a sign, is enough. It was instituted by the example and the practice of our Master, to remain in force till his second coming. It was instituted with blessing and giving of thanks, to be a memorial of Christ's death. Frequent mention is made of his precious blood, as the price of our redemption. How comfortable is this to poor repenting sinners, that the blood of Christ is shed for many! If for many, why not for me? It was a sign of the conveyance of the benefits purchased for us by his death. Apply the doctrine of Christ crucified to yourselves; let it be meat and drink to your souls, strengthening and refreshing your spiritual life. It was to be an earnest and foretaste of the happiness of heaven, and thereby to put us out of taste for the pleasures and delights of sense. Every one that has tasted spiritual delights, straightway desires eternal ones. Though the great Shepherd passed through his sufferings without one false step, yet his followers often have been scattered by the small measure of sufferings allotted to them. How very apt we are to think well of ourselves, and to trust our own hearts! It was ill done of Peter thus to answer his Master, and not with fear and trembling. Lord, give me grace to keep me from denying thee.
[Mark.14.32-Mark.14.42]
Verses 32-42
Christ's sufferings began with the sorest of all, those in his soul. He began to be sorely amazed; words not used in St. Matthew, but very full of meaning. The terrors of God set themselves in array against him, and he allowed him to contemplate them. Never was sorrow like unto his at this time. Now he was made a curse for us; the curses of the law were laid upon him as our Surety. He now tasted death, in all the bitterness of it. This was that fear of which the apostle speaks, the natural fear of pain and death, at which human nature startles. Can we ever entertain favourable, or even slight thoughts of sin, when we see the painful sufferings which sin, though but reckoned to him, brought on the Lord Jesus? Shall that sit light upon our souls, which sat so heavy upon his? Was Christ in such agony for our sins, and shall we never be in agony about them? How should we look upon Him whom we have pierced, and mourn! It becomes us to be exceedingly sorrowful for sin, because He was so, and never to mock at it. Christ, as Man, pleaded, that, if it were possible, his sufferings might pass from him. As Mediator, he submitted to the will of God, saying, Nevertheless, not what I will, but what thou wilt; I bid it welcome. See how the sinful weakness of Christ's disciples returns, and overpowers them. What heavy clogs these bodies of ours are to our souls! But when we see trouble at the door, we should get ready for it. Alas, even believers often look at the Redeemer's sufferings in a drowsy manner, and instead of being ready to die with Christ, they are not even prepared to watch with him one hour.
[Mark.14.43-Mark.14.52]
Verses 43-52
Because Christ appeared not as a temporal prince, but preached repentance, reformation, and a holy life, and directed men's thoughts, and affections, and aims to another world, therefore the Jewish rulers sought to destroy him. Peter wounded one of the band. It is easier to fight for Christ than to die for him. But there is a great difference between faulty disciples and hypocrites. The latter rashly and without thought call Christ Master, and express great affection for him, yet betray him to his enemies. Thus they hasten their own destruction.
[Mark.14.53-Mark.14.65]
Verses 53-65
We have here Christ's condemnation before the great council of the Jews. Peter followed; but the high priest's fire-side was no proper place, nor his servants proper company, for Peter: it was an entrance into temptation. Great diligence was used to procure false witnesses against Jesus, yet their testimony was not equal to the charge of a capital crime, by the utmost stretch of their law. He was asked, Art thou the Son of the Blessed? that is, the Son of God. For the proof of his being the Son of God, he refers to his second coming. In these outrages we have proofs of man's enmity to God, and of God's free and unspeakable love to man.
[Mark.14.66-Mark.14.72]
Verses 66-72
Peter's denying Christ began by keeping at a distance from him. Those that are shy of godliness, are far in the way to deny Christ. Those who think it dangerous to be in company with Christ's disciples, because thence they may be drawn in to suffer for him, will find it much more dangerous to be in company with his enemies, because there they may be drawn in to sin against him. When Christ was admired and flocked after, Peter readily owned him; but will own no relation to him now he is deserted and despised. Yet observe, Peter's repentance was very speedy. Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall; and let him that has fallen think of these things, and of his own offences, and return to the Lord with weeping and supplication, seeking forgiveness, and to be raised up by the Holy Spirit.

Christ stands before Pilate (verses 1–14)

They bound Jesus.

We should often remember our Lord's bonds, remembering the One who was bound for us, and reckon ourselves bound with him.

By handing over their King, the religious leaders effectively handed over the kingdom of God. By their own action, it would be taken from them and entrusted to another nation.

Jesus answered Pilate directly but did not answer the witnesses. Their accusations were known to be false, and even Pilate was convinced of their falsehood.

Pilate hoped to appeal from the priests to the people, expecting the crowd to rescue Jesus from the religious leaders' demands.

But the priests stirred up the people still more. They cried for Jesus to be crucified.

We should judge people and events by their real character and by God's word, not by popular rumors.

No person ever received such disgraceful treatment as Jesus, the only perfectly wise, holy and excellent man ever to walk the earth.

Contemplating his mistreatment should give us a strong sense of humanity's wickedness and hostility to God and teach us to hate the sinful motives displayed by his persecutors.

Jesus is led out to be crucified (verses 15–21)

Jesus encountered death in one of its most terrifying forms: the death reserved for the worst criminals.

The cross brought shame.

Because sin had dishonored God, Christ made satisfaction by accepting the greatest disgrace human nature could bear.

Crucifixion was also regarded as a cursed death under the law (Deuteronomy 21:23).

Roman soldiers mocked Jesus as a king, just as the high priest's servants had mocked him as prophet and Savior.

Can a Christian be proud of splendid purple or scarlet clothing when such garments were used to mock Christ?

He wore the crown of thorns that we deserved, so that we might wear the crown of glory that he earned.

Sin made us liable to everlasting shame and contempt. To deliver us, Jesus freely submitted to shame and contempt.

He was led out among evildoers, though he himself had committed no sin.

The suffering of the meek and holy Redeemer continually teaches believers, who should never become weary of considering it.

After seeing what Jesus endured, how can I, a guilty sinner, indulge angry complaints, reproaches or threats when I experience harm or hardship?

Jesus is crucified (verses 22–32)

The place of Jesus' crucifixion was called the place of a skull, the customary place of execution. He was counted among transgressors in every respect.

When we look at Christ crucified, remember what was written above him: he is a King.

We must therefore submit ourselves to him as his true subjects.

Two thieves were crucified beside him, with Jesus in the middle, to deepen his humiliation.

Yet Scripture had foretold that he would be counted among transgressors because he was made sin for us.

Passersby insulted him.

They demanded that he come down from the cross before they would believe. But when he gave an even more convincing sign by rising from the grave, they still did not believe.

Anyone who truly understands the salvation purchased by the Son of God's suffering and death will seek it earnestly.

The first hope of pardon and eternal life produces thanksgiving, and the sins that brought the Lord of glory to the cross produce godly sorrow.

Christ dies (verses 33–41)

Thick darkness covered the land from noon until three in the afternoon.

The people were trying to extinguish the Sun of Righteousness.

The darkness signified the deep cloud over Christ's human soul when he offered himself for sin.

Jesus did not complain here that his disciples had forsaken him, but that his Father had forsaken him.

Especially in this suffering he was made sin for us.

Paul could rejoice even when describing his life as a sacrifice poured out in the service of the saints (Philippians 2:17).

But being offered as a sacrifice for sinners' sins was something incomparably greater.

At the instant Jesus died, the temple veil tore from top to bottom.

For unbelieving Jews, Henry takes this as an alarming sign of judgment upon their temple order and nation.

For believers, it declares the opening of a new and living way into God's holiest presence through Jesus' blood.

The centurion seems to have been deeply moved by the confidence with which Jesus had spoken to God as Father and entrusted his spirit to him.

Rightly understanding the crucified Christ reconciles believers to the thought of dying. They long to see, love and praise the Savior who was pierced and wounded to rescue them from the coming judgment.

Jesus is buried (verses 42–47)

We now stand beside the burial of our Lord.

May we, by grace, be united to him in the likeness of his burial.

Joseph of Arimathea was waiting for God's kingdom.

Those who hope to share that kingdom's blessings must be ready to acknowledge Christ's cause even when it seems utterly defeated.

God raised up Joseph to serve him at this moment.

Providence also ensured that Pilate investigated carefully whether Jesus had actually died. This removed any plausible claim that Jesus had merely survived the crucifixion.

Pilate gave Joseph permission to take the body down and bury it.

Some women watched where Jesus was laid because they intended to return after the Sabbath and anoint his body; there had been no time beforehand.

The exact location of the tomb mattered especially because Jesus would rise again.

He will not abandon those who trust and call upon him.

Death has lost its sting for the believer. It will soon end their sorrows, as it brought an end to the Savior's earthly sufferings.

Verses 1-14
They bound Christ. It is good for us often to remember the bonds of the Lord Jesus, as bound with him who was bound for us. By delivering up the King, they, in effect, delivered up the kingdom of God, which was, therefore, as by their own consent, taken from them, and given to another nation. Christ gave Pilate a direct answer, but would not answer the witnesses, because the things they alleged were known to be false, even Pilate himself was convinced they were so. Pilate thought that he might appeal from the priests to the people, and that they would deliver Jesus out of the priests' hands. But they were more and more urged by the priests, and cried, Crucify him! Crucify him! Let us judge of persons and things by their merits, and the standard of God's word, and not by common report. The thought that no one ever was so shamefully treated, as the only perfectly wise, holy, and excellent Person that ever appeared on earth, leads the serious mind to strong views of man's wickedness and enmity to God. Let us more and more abhor the evil dispositions which marked the conduct of these persecutors.
[Mark.15.15-Mark.15.21]
Verses 15-21
Christ met death in its greatest terror. It was the death of the vilest malefactors. Thus the cross and the shame are put together. God having been dishonoured by the sin of man, Christ made satisfaction by submitting to the greatest disgrace human nature could be loaded with. It was a cursed death; thus it was branded by the Jewish law, [Deut.21.23] De 21:23. The Roman soldiers mocked our Lord Jesus as a King; thus in the high priest's hall the servants had mocked him as a Prophet and Saviour. Shall a purple or scarlet robe be matter of pride to a Christian, which was matter of reproach and shame to Christ? He wore the crown of thorns which we deserved, that we might wear the crown of glory which he merited. We were by sin liable to everlasting shame and contempt; to deliver us, our Lord Jesus submitted to shame and contempt. He was led forth with the workers of iniquity, though he did no sin. The sufferings of the meek and holy Redeemer, are ever a source of instruction to the believer, of which, in his best hours, he cannot be weary. Did Jesus thus suffer, and shall I, a vile sinner, fret or repine? Shall I indulge anger, or utter reproaches and threats because of troubles and injuries?
[Mark.15.22-Mark.15.32]
Verses 22-32
The place where our Lord Jesus was crucified, was called the place of a scull; it was the common place of execution; for he was in all respects numbered with the transgressors. Whenever we look unto Christ crucified, we must remember what was written over his head; he is a King, and we must give up ourselves to be his subjects, as Israelites indeed. They crucified two thieves with him, and him in the midst; they thereby intended him great dishonour. But it was foretold that he should be numbered with the transgressors, because he was made sin for us. Even those who passed by railed at him. They told him to come down from the cross, and they would believe; but they did not believe, though he gave them a more convincing sign when he came up from the grave. With what earnestness will the man who firmly believes the truth, as made known by the sufferings of Christ, seek for salvation! With what gratitude will he receive the dawning hope of forgiveness and eternal life, as purchased for him by the sufferings and death of the Son of God! and with what godly sorrow will he mourn over the sins which crucified the Lord of glory!
[Mark.15.33-Mark.15.41]
Verses 33-41
There was a thick darkness over the land, from noon until three in the afternoon. The Jews were doing their utmost to extinguish the Sun of Righteousness. The darkness signified the cloud which the human soul of Christ was under, when he was making it an offering for sin. He did not complain that his disciples forsook him, but that his Father forsook him. In this especially he was made sin for us. When Paul was to be offered as a sacrifice for the service saints, he could joy and rejoice, [Phil.2.17] Php 2:17; but it is another thing to be offered as a sacrifice for the sin of sinners. At the same instant that Jesus died, the veil of the temple was rent from the top to the bottom. This spake terror to the unbelieving Jews, and was a sign of the destruction of their church and nation. It speaks comfort to all believing Christians, for it signified the laying open a new and living way into the holiest by the blood of Jesus. The confidence with which Christ had openly addressed God as his Father, and committed his soul into his hands, seems greatly to have affected the centurion. Right views of Christ crucified will reconcile the believer to the thought of death; he longs to behold, love, and praise, as he ought, that Saviour who was wounded and pierced to save him from the wrath to come.
[Mark.15.42-Mark.15.47]
Verses 42-47
We are here attending the burial of our Lord Jesus. Oh that we may by grace be planted in the likeness of it! Joseph of Arimathea was one who waited for the kingdom of God. Those who hope for a share in its privileges, must own Christ's cause, when it seems to be crushed. This man God raised up for his service. There was a special providence, that Pilate should be so strict in his inquiry, that there might be no pretence to say Jesus was alive. Pilate gave Joseph leave to take down the body, and do what he pleased with it. Some of the women beheld where Jesus was laid, that they might come after the sabbath to anoint the dead body, because they had not time to do it before. Special notice was taken of Christ's sepulchre, because he was to rise again. And he will not forsake those who trust in him, and call upon him. Death, deprived of its sting, will soon end the believer's sorrows, as it ended those of the Saviour.

The women learn that Jesus has risen (verses 1–8)

Nicodemus had brought many spices for Jesus' burial, yet the faithful women wanted to bring their own. Another person's demonstration of love for Christ should never prevent us from showing our own love.

Those whose devotion moves them to seek Jesus diligently often find that seemingly insurmountable obstacles are removed.

When we accept trouble and expense out of love for Christ, he accepts the devotion even if our plans do not succeed.

The sight of the angel ought to have encouraged the women, but instead they were frightened. We often turn what should comfort us into a cause for fear through our own misunderstanding.

Jesus was crucified, but now he is glorified. He is risen; he is no longer in the tomb, but alive again.

They would see him again. For now, they could look at the place where he had lain.

Those mourning for Jesus will receive encouragement at the proper time.

The angel named Peter particularly. This news would be precious to someone deeply grieved by his own sin.

Seeing Christ is a welcome comfort for a true penitent; and a truly repentant person is welcome before Christ.

The women went quickly to tell the disciples. Yet troubling fear may hinder us from serving Christ and other people as we would if our faith and joy were stronger.

Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene and other disciples (verses 9–13)

There can be no better news for grieving disciples than the announcement that Christ has risen.

We should seek to comfort sorrowing believers by telling them what we have learned of Jesus.

In God's wise Providence, proofs of the resurrection were given gradually and received cautiously. This made the apostles' later confident testimony more convincing.

Yet how slowly we accept the comfort offered by God's word!

While Jesus consoles his people, he may also need to rebuke their hardness of heart, both for doubting his promises and for failing to obey his commands.

Jesus commissions the apostles (verses 14–18)

The evidence confirming the gospel is abundant. People who reject it may be rightly rebuked for unbelief.

Jesus confirmed the calling of the eleven apostles and instructed them to take the gospel into all the world, preaching it to every creature.

Only those who are truly Christians are saved through Christ.

Simon Magus professed faith and received baptism, yet was later described as remaining bound in wickedness (Acts 8:13–25).

The faith that saves receives Christ in all his offices and characters, trusting him for every purpose of salvation.

It produces corresponding effects in the heart and life. Mere intellectual assent is dead faith and cannot save.

The commission reaches every creature throughout the world.

The gospel's message includes not only truths, invitations, encouragements and commands, but also solemn warnings.

The apostles received powers to perform miracles that confirmed the teaching they preached and assisted its spread among nations that had not heard it.

Christ ascends into heaven (verses 19 and 20)

After speaking to the apostles, Jesus ascended into heaven.

His sitting signifies both rest and royal authority.

He has finished his work and taken possession of his kingdom.

To sit at God's right hand declares his sovereign dignity and universal power.

Everything God does for us, gives us or accepts from us is through his Son, who is now glorified with the glory he possessed before the world existed.

The apostles went out preaching everywhere, near and far.

Their message was heavenly and spiritual, opposed to the world's ordinary desires, and met with great resistance.

They possessed none of the usual worldly supports for such a mission. Nevertheless, within a few years the gospel was announced across the known world.

Ministers today, Henry says, do not need to perform miracles to prove their message. Scripture's divine origin has already been confirmed, leaving people responsible for accepting or rejecting its testimony.

The changes the gospel continually produces when faithfully preached and genuinely believed—transforming human character and conduct—remain a constant and, in Henry's language, miraculous proof that the gospel is God's power for salvation to believers.

Verses 1-8
Nicodemus brought a large quantity of spices, but these good women did not think that enough. The respect others show to Christ, should not hinder us from showing our respect. And those who are carried by holy zeal, to seek Christ diligently, will find the difficulties in their way speedily vanish. When we put ourselves to trouble and expense, from love to Christ, we shall be accepted, though our endeavours are not successful. The sight of the angel might justly have encouraged them, but they were affrighted. Thus many times that which should be matter of comfort to us, through our own mistake, proves a terror to us. He was crucified, but he is glorified. He is risen, he is not here, not dead, but alive again; hereafter you will see him, but you may here see the place where he was laid. Thus seasonable comforts will be sent to those that lament after the Lord Jesus. Peter is particularly named, Tell Peter; it will be most welcome to him, for he is in sorrow for sin. A sight of Christ will be very welcome to a true penitent, and a true penitent is very welcome to a sight of Christ. The men ran with all the haste they could to the disciples; but disquieting fears often hinder us from doing that service to Christ and to the souls of men, which, if faith and the joy of faith were strong, we might do.
[Mark.16.9-Mark.16.13]
Verses 9-13
Better news cannot be brought to disciples in tears, than to tell them of Christ's resurrection. And we should study to comfort disciples that are mourners, by telling them whatever we have seen of Christ. It was a wise providence that the proofs of Christ's resurrection were given gradually, and admitted cautiously, that the assurance with which the apostles preached this doctrine afterwards might the more satisfy. Yet how slowly do we admit the consolations which the word of God holds forth! Therefore while Christ comforts his people, he often sees it needful to rebuke and correct them for hardness of heart in distrusting his promise, as well as in not obeying his holy precepts.
[Mark.16.14-Mark.16.18]
Verses 14-18
The evidences of the truth of the gospel are so full, that those who receive it not, may justly be upbraided with their unbelief. Our blessed Lord renewed his choice of the eleven as his apostles, and commissioned them to go into all the world, to preach his gospel to every creature. Only he that is a true Christian shall be saved through Christ. Simon Magus professed to believe, and was baptized, yet he was declared to be in the bonds of iniquity: see his history in [Acts.8.13-Acts.8.25] Ac 8:13-25. Doubtless this is a solemn declaration of that true faith which receives Christ in all his characters and offices, and for all the purposes of salvation, and which produces its right effect on the heart and life; not a mere assent, which is a dead faith, and cannot profit. The commission of Christ's ministers extends to every creature throughout the world, and the declarations of the gospel contain not only truths, encouragements, and precepts, but also most awful warnings. Observe what power the apostles should be endued with, for confirming the doctrine they were to preach. These were miracles to confirm the truth of the gospel, and means of spreading the gospel among nations that had not heard it.
[Mark.16.19-Mark.16.20]
Verses 19-20
After the Lord had spoken he went up into heaven. Sitting is a posture of rest, he had finished his work; and a posture of rule, he took possession of his kingdom. He sat at the right hand of God, which denotes his sovereign dignity and universal power. Whatever God does concerning us, gives to us, or accepts from us, it is by his Son. Now he is glorified with the glory he had before the world. The apostles went forth, and preached every where, far and near. Though the doctrine they preached was spiritual and heavenly, and directly contrary to the spirit and temper of the world; though it met with much opposition, and was wholly destitute of all worldly supports and advantages; yet in a few years the sound went forth unto the ends of the earth. Christ's ministers do not now need to work miracles to prove their message; the Scriptures are proved to be of Divine origin, and this renders those without excuse who reject or neglect them. The effects of the gospel, when faithfully preached, and truly believed, in changing the tempers and characters of mankind, form a constant proof, a miraculous proof, that the gospel is the power of God unto salvation, of all who believe.
